etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English removen, from Anglo-Norman remover, removeir, from Old French remouvoir, from Latin removēre, from re- + movēre (“to move”), equivalent to re- +‎ move. Displaced native Old English āfierran.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, formal) To replace a dish within a course.

quote.citation: 1959, Georgette Heyer, chapter 1, in The Unknown Ajax:
quote.text: But Richmond […] appeared to lose himself in his own reflections. Some pickled crab, which he had not touched, had been removed with a damson pie; and his sister saw […] that he had eaten no more than a spoonful of that either.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To move from one place to another, especially to take away.

quote.citation: 1530 January 27 (Gregorian calendar), W[illiam] T[yndale], transl., [The Pentateuch] (Tyndale Bible), Malborow [Marburg], Hesse:  […]  Hans Luft [actually Antwerp: Johan Hoochstraten], →OCLC, Deuteronomye xix:[14], folio XXXV, recto:
quote.text: Thou ſhalt not remoue thy neghbours marke which they of olde tyme haue ſett in thyne enheritaunce that thou enheretteſt in the londe which the Lorde thy God geueth the to enioye it.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Dangerous Lady”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC, page 36:
quote.text: Now that she was rested and had fed from the luncheon tray Mrs. Broome had just removed, she had reverted to her normal gaiety.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To discard, set aside, especially something abstract (a thought, feeling, etc.).

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 524:
quote.text: Eternall thraldom was to her more liefe, / Then loſſe of chaſtitie, or chaunge of loue : / Dye had ſhe rather in tormenting griefe, / Then any ſhould of falſeneſſe her reproue, / Or looſeneſſe, that ſhe lightly did remoue.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Karen McVeigh, “US rules human genes can't be patented”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 10:
quote.text: The US supreme court has ruled unanimously that natural human genes cannot be patented, a decision that scientists and civil rights campaigners said removed a major barrier to patient care and medical innovation.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, now rare) To depart, to leave; to move oneself or be moved.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “vj”, in Le Morte Darthur, book V:
quote.text: THenne the kynge dyd doo calle syre Gawayne / syre Borce / syr Lyonel and syre Bedewere / and commaunded them to goo strayte to syre Lucius / and saye ye to hym that hastely he remeue oute of my land / And yf he wil not / bydde hym make hym redy to bataylle and not distresse the poure peple(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: 1855, Francis Kildale Robinson, A Glossary of Yorkshire Words and Phrases: Collected in Whitby and the Neighbourhood. With Examples of Their Colloquial Use, and Allusions to Local Customs and Trditions, page 129:
quote.text: […]  you shall set your stakes at the brim of the water, each a yard apart, and so yedder them with your yedders, and so stake them with your strut stowers, that they may stand three tides without removing by the force thereof.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To change one's residence or place of business; to move.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane.

quote.citation: 1719 May 6 (Gregorian calendar), [Daniel Defoe], The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Taylor […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Now my life began to be so easy that I began to say to myself that could I but have been safe from more savages, I cared not if I was never to remove from the place where I lived.

quote.citation: 1834, David Crockett, A Narrative of the Life of, Nebraska, published 1987, page 20:
quote.text: Shortly after this, my father removed, and settled in the same county, about ten miles above Greenville.

quote.citation: 1886, Lim Hiong Seng, Handbook of the Swatow Vernacular, Singapore: Koh Yew Hean Press:
quote.text: I am going to remove. / Where are you going to remove to? / I don't know yet. / When will you know?

quote.citation: 1925, W. K. & Co., “How to Avoid a Controversy Over Fixtures Between Landlord and Tenant”, in American Independent Baker: Official Organ of the Retail Bakers, volume 23, page 20:
quote.text: About a year ago we removed to the above address, which we leased on a five-year lease with privilege of cancellation in one year.

definitions.definition: To dismiss or discharge from office.

quote.citation: [1644], [John Milton], Of Education. To Master Samuel Hartlib, [London:  […]  Thomas Underhill and/or Thomas Johnson], →OCLC:
quote.text: This place should be at once both school and university, not needing a remove to any other house of scholarship.

quote.citation: 1764 December 19 (indicated as 1765), Oliver Goldsmith, The Traveller, or A Prospect of Society. A Poem. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Newbery, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: And drags at each remove a lengthening chain.

quote.citation: 1761, John Mordant, The Complete Steward:
quote.text: There is no tree admits of transplantation so well as the Elm, for a tree of twenty years growth will admit of a remove.

definitions.definition: (cooking, now chiefly historical) A dish served to replace an earlier one during a meal; a part of a new course.

quote.citation: 1796, Mary Wollstonecraft, Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark, Oxford, published 2009, page 16:
quote.text: A supper brings up the rear, not forgetting the introductory luncheon, almost equalling in removes the dinner.

quote.citation: 1842, [Katherine] Thomson, chapter XIII, in Widows and Widowers. A Romance of Real Life., volume I, London: Richard Bentley, […], →OCLC, page 289:
quote.text: An attempt at entrées and removes failed at the first dinner-party.

definitions.definition: (British) (at some public schools) A division of the school, especially the form prior to last
A step or gradation (as in the phrase "at one remove")

quote.citation: 1716 January 3 (Gregorian calendar), Joseph Addison, “The Free-holder: No. 1. Friday, December 23. 1715.”, in The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq; […], volume IV, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], published 1721, →OCLC:
quote.text: A freeholder is but one remove from a legislator.

quote.citation: 1739, [David Hume], “Of the Connexion or Association of Ideas”, in A Treatise of Human Nature: […], book I (Of the Understanding), London:  […]  John Noon, […], →OCLC, part I (Of Ideas; Their Origin, Composition, Connexion, Abstraction, &c.), page 28:
quote.text: That vve may underſtand the full extent of theſe relations, vve must conſider, that tvvo objects are connected together in the imagination, not only vvhen the one is immediately reſembling, contiguous to, or the cauſe of the other, but alſo vvhen there is interpoſed betwixt them a third object, vvhich bears to both of them any of theſe relations. This may be carried on to a great length; tho' at the ſame time vve may obſerve, that each remove conſiderably vveakens the relation.

quote.citation: 1822, Paul Brown, “Of the Degrees of Faith, according to probability, and force of impression”, in A Disquisition on Faith, Washington, D.C.:  […]  [F]or the Author[, b]y Andrew Way, page 24:
quote.text: Thus though this degree of faith is but one remove from disbelief, (denial) nevertheless as much probability is given to one side of the question as the other, and we stand, as it were, on an average between two.

quote.citation: 2007, James D. McCallister, King's Highway, page 162:
quote.text: In his unfortunate absence at this far remove of 2007, Zevon's musicianship and irascible wit are as missed as ever.

quote.citation: 2022 September 9, HarryBlank, “The Mausoleum at Ipperwash”, in SCP Foundation‎[1], archived from the original on 27 May 2024:
quote.text: They were standing in the foreshortened airlock approach now, having just left a gaggle of nervous techs and agents behind the sealed bulkhead. Nobody knew what they were about to unleash, so it was best to keep it as many removes from the rest of the Site as was possible. When they opened the vault door, the filtration systems would whir to life and start sifting the air for esoteric elements. Ibanez suspected it would be months before the approach was considered clean, the doors retracted and active air and pedestrian circulation restored.

definitions.definition: Distance in time or space; interval.

quote.citation: 1654, Richard Whitlock, Zootomia; Or, Observations on the Present Manners of the English:
quote.text: How many Masters have some stately Houses had, in the age of a small Cottage, that hath, as it were, lived, and dyed with her old Master, both dropping down together. Such vain Preservatories of us, are our Inheritances, even once removed: but look on it more Removes off, and continuing in thy Name, yet how little doth that concerne Thee (though the first Purchaser, or his Heire) Lazy Posterity, when they heare it so called know it by the Name, but not as thine;  […]

definitions.definition: (figurative, by extension) Emotional distance or indifference.
(figurative, by extension) State of mind allowing for a certain degree of objectivity in evaluating things.

quote.citation: 2021 October 19, David Graeber, David Wengrowr, “Unfreezing the ice age: the truth about humanity’s deep past”, in The Guardian, UK:
quote.text: The fact that one structure applied in the rainy season and another in the dry allowed Nambikwara chiefs to view their own social arrangements at one remove: to see them as not simply “given”, in the natural order of things, but as something at least partially open to human intervention.

definitions.definition: (dated) The transfer of one's home or business to another place; a move.

quote.citation: 1855, John Henry Newman, Callista:
quote.text: It is an English proverb that three removes are as bad as a fire.

definitions.definition: The act of resetting a horse's shoe.

quote.citation: 1731 (date written, published 1745), Jonathan Swift, “Directions to Servants”, in Thomas Sheridan, John Nichols, editors, The Works of the Rev. Jonathan Swift, […], new edition, volume XVI, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], published 1801, →OCLC:
quote.text: His horse wanted two removes; your horse wanted nails
